Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

reference notes

Mara Ellison and her brother Theo are sorting photographs inherited from their grandmother June. The collection is shared by six relatives, but Mara is coordinating the work from a house in Eugene, Oregon. June took pictures from the late 1950s through 2018, and the boxes also include prints from earlier generations. The family wants a usable archive, not a public gallery. Mara has a Windows desktop with a 4 TB internal drive, Theo uses a MacBook, and their cousin Lina mostly works from an Android phone. They can gather at Mara’s house once a month, usually on a Sunday afternoon, but they do most coordination by email.

The current material is uneven. There are about 3,800 digital files in several folders, including camera originals, phone images, scans, and exported pictures that relatives have already edited. Two old USB drives contain overlapping folders, though nobody has compared them carefully. A shoebox holds around 450 prints, a small envelope holds 30 negatives, and three albums have handwritten captions. June’s albums often identify people by first name only. A pencilled note inside one album says, “These were taken after the move, but I can’t remember which summer.” The family thinks the move was in 1974 or 1975, but there is no confirmed date.

Mara made test scans of twelve prints with a flatbed scanner at 600 dpi, saving uncompressed TIFF files. She also scanned two album pages as JPEGs to preserve their layout. Some prints have writing on the back, and Mara photographed those backs separately. She has not decided whether the back images should be stored beside the front scans, combined into a multipage file, or linked another way. The negatives have not been scanned. One print has a torn corner; another has a faint date stamp that could read either 1963 or 1968. No one wants the scanning process to flatten, crop, or discard handwritten marks.

The digital folders are named things like “June old laptop,” “phone dump 2,” and “photos to sort.” File dates are not always trustworthy: a group of pictures was copied from a CD in 2012, and the displayed dates then became the copy date. Theo remembers that the pictures were originally taken during a 2006 camping trip near Bend. Lina has a message from June identifying one picture as “the picnic where the dog stole the sandwiches,” but the message does not identify the year. Preserve original filenames where practical, and make any renamed copies traceable to those filenames. If a date comes only from the album’s placement or a relative’s uncertain memory, distinguish it from a date recorded by a camera or written on the print.

There are privacy and access questions. A few photographs show children who are now adults, and one folder includes family members who have asked not to have their images posted on social media. The archive should remain for family use. Mara proposes that she and Theo can manage files, while Lina and the other relatives can browse and contribute corrections. Nobody has settled whether every relative should be able to download high-resolution copies. Theo wants to avoid making a private link that can be forwarded indefinitely. Mara said, “I’d rather explain a missing photo than find the whole collection in a search result.” The family has not chosen an online service, and nobody has agreed to pay for a particular subscription.

Two incidents make backup planning important. In 2021, a laptop failure took several weeks of sorting notes with it; some pictures survived on a phone, but the notes did not. Last winter, Mara accidentally deleted a folder while clearing space, then recovered most of it from an old drive. The recovered folder had no clear indication of which files were original and which had been edited. The relatives would like a dependable way to keep more than one copy and to notice when files have changed, but they have not specified a cloud provider or a budget. A family member can store a drive at Theo’s home, about 90 miles away, and bring it to the monthly gathering for updates.

A few details from conversations should stay attached to the right people and events. Theo recalls June saying, “If I wrote a name on the back, I was sure then, but ask Mara before you label the cousins.” Lina remembers June calling a particular garden picture “the first year the lilacs came back.” Mara thinks that picture may be from 1992, but is not certain. One album has a caption, “Easter at Aunt Rose’s, maybe 1967,” and the location is not confirmed. The family has agreed that uncertain identifications should remain visibly uncertain rather than being silently converted into facts. There are no known professional studio negatives, and the relatives have not yet decided whether they want face recognition or other automated tagging.

A printed inventory from Mara’s first sorting afternoon records these groups: a blue tin with 86 color prints from June’s kitchen; album one with 42 pages and captions on 19 pages; a bundle of 63 loose black-and-white prints marked “Ellison / before Oregon”; the two USB drives; 114 phone photos received from Lina; and a folder of 27 images that Theo edited to brighten shadows. Those counts are rough and may overlap. The inventory was written before the second USB drive was opened. Mara also found 14 duplicate-looking images in the phone folder, but has not established whether they are exact file duplicates or separate shots taken seconds apart.

The following configuration snippet was copied from Mara’s draft notes:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 56
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"

1. Keep the physical and digital sources distinguishable. The family can store print scans and digital originals in the same overall archive if their source and handling history remain clear. Do not assume that every scan should replace the corresponding print, or that a brightened edit is the only version worth keeping. The archive needs a way to relate an image of a print’s back to its front without erasing the original files.

2. Treat names, dates, captions, and locations as information with varying confidence. Existing handwriting and direct quotations matter, even when they contain uncertainty. The “after the move” note is not a verified year, and the possible 1963/1968 stamp is unresolved. A date imported from a CD or copied folder may describe file transfer rather than when a photograph was taken. Keep those distinctions visible in any proposed metadata or folder approach.

3. Plan for family access without assuming public sharing. The six relatives need a workable way to view the collection and contribute corrections, but their roles and download permissions are undecided. Keep the stated wish for family-only access in view, and do not presume a vendor, subscription, or permanent share-link arrangement. The requests about children’s images and social media should inform the discussion.

4. The monthly gathering is a realistic opportunity for scanning, review, and drive exchanges, while email remains the usual coordination method. Any proposed process should account for the mixed Windows, Mac, and Android devices, the remote copy at Theo’s home, and the lessons from the lost notes and accidental deletion. The family has not set a spending limit.
